name: Google Cloud TPU v4 / v5e / v5p (per chip-hour, in a pod)
region: us-central1 (v5e, v4), us-east1 and us-east5 (v5p, v6e), plus europe-west1/4, asia-northeast1, asia-southeast1, us-south1
price_basis: PER CHIP-HOUR in USD, not per VM - Google states this explicitly. v5e $1.20/chip-h on-demand (us-central1, us-east5, us-west1, us-west4); $1.416 us-south1 Dallas; $1.32132 europe-west1; $1.56 europe-west4 and asia-southeast1. v5p $4.20/chip-h (us-east5, us-east1). v4 $3.22/chip-h (us-central2). v6e Trillium $2.70 (us-east1, us-east5). DWS Flex-start halves v5e to $0.60 and v5p to $2.10; 3-year commitment takes v5e to $0.54 and v5p to $1.89. Published 2026-10-03. PRICE CLASS: this is a PUBLISHED LIST PRICE - an asking rate a new customer is quoted, not a realised, discounted or negotiated transaction rate. A real bill is at or below this and typically well below it once commitments, credits and committed-use discounts are applied.
notes:
Cloud TPU is the cheapest credible accelerator hour in this slice on a like-for-like basis: TPU v5e at $1.20 per chip-hour is less than AWS g6's L4 ($1.67) and far under any H100 hour, and v5p at $4.20 is under AWS p5's on-demand $6.88. But three structural caveats make it NOT a drop-in substitute for a GPU hour. (1) UNIT: the price is per CHIP inside a pod, and the page warns that the console displays VM-hours - a v4 host with 4 chips shows as $12.88/h which is exactly 4 x $3.22 - so reading the console figure as a per-VM price understates by the chip count, and the minimum billable object is a slice, not a chip. (2) QUOTA, not payment, is the gate: the page directs you to the Cloud TPU quota policy to learn how to request quota, so availability is lead-time-bound, not credit-bound. (3) Portability: XLA/JAX only. Every engine, kernel and quantization path elsewhere in this repo is CUDA-shaped. Also note the discount ladder here is the deepest in the whole slice - DWS Flex-start at 50% off on-demand and a 3-year commitment at 55% off for v5e - and unlike GCP's accelerator-optimized VMs, TPU consumption does carry 1-year and 3-year CUDs. TPU v4 and v3 are legacy pods; Ironwood at $12.00/chip-h in us-central1 is the newest and by far the most expensive per chip.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04): this is a first-party silicon SKUs record (AWS Trainium / Google TPU) - non-US-origin designs that are not classified under the US ECCN 3A090 advanced-computing regime at all. Recorded null deliberately rather than false: the EAR does not govern the part, so the relevant controls are AWS's and Google's own regional service-availability policies plus the destination's import rules, which this repo has no primary source for. Do NOT read null here as 'unrestricted'. Sources for why a null is the honest answer rather than a gap: spl-eccn-3a090-ccl (the US regime whose scope is defined by US-origin classification), spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance (end-user/parent screening, which applies to where the customer is rather than to which silicon is supplied).

 LEAD TIME: null, and correct as null. For a listed on-demand instance type the provisioning delay is effectively zero - capacity is allocated per request - so a week count would be meaningless; the real gate for scarce shapes is either a quota increase or a capacity reservation, not a lead time. Where a published commitment horizon exists it IS recorded: AWS documents that a Capacity Block may be reserved with a start time up to EIGHT WEEKS in the future (source spl-aws-capacity-block-booking-horizon), which is a floor on how far ahead scarce capacity must be committed, not a wait. On-demand and Spot tiers publish no lead time at all; their constraint is availability, and the repo records that as availability=in-stock or a spot/reality note rather than as a fabricated week figure. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
